transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-01-28
Time: 10:00 AM PT (18:00Z)
Duration: ~46 minutes
Attendees: Alex Moreno (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Miguel Alvarez (Aurora BE), Sara Bennett (Aurora CTO), Tanya Li (Aurora SRE)

Summary:
Aurora Logistics is evaluating Redwood for a routing assistant that must handle surges (driver check-ins + route re-plans) with tight p95 latency SLOs and streaming token responses to mobile clients. Primary concerns: hitting p95 < 250ms for short responses during peak bursts, predictable behavior under concurrency (500-2,000 concurrent streams), and data residency/KMS for PII in routes. They want a side-by-side token/sec benchmark on Hosted vs Dedicated; on-prem/private is a potential later step.

Topics:
- p95 targets and what contributes to tail latency
- streaming vs non-streaming token throughput
- concurrency models and autoscaling tradeoffs
- KV cache/prefix caching, quantization impacts on quality
- security: SOC 2, KMS, VPC peering

Action items (recorded here and in metadata): see action_items

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Alex Moreno from Redwood, AE on this account. With me is Priya, our systems SE who'll dive into the latency profiling details. How are you all?
[00:08] Sara: Good, thanks. Quick note, we'll need a short recording for our internal notes.
[00:11] Alex: Yep recorded — Fireflies on. Miguel, Tanya, feel free to jump in.
[00:16] Miguel: Hey, thanks. So high level, we run driver routing + incident replan. We get large spikes when bad weather hits — like 4x normal traffic for 10-20 minutes, and we need the UI to remain snappy.
[00:28] Priya: Got it. When you say snappy, are you targetting p95 for the whole round-trip, or p95 for server-side generation?
[00:34] Miguel: Ideally p95 end-to-end under 250ms for short 10-40 token replies — most messages are confirmations or short reroutes. We have longer planning calls too but those are lower cadence.
[00:44] Tanya: And we have around 600 concurrent active drivers during peaks today, could be more as we expand.
[00:50] Alex: Good context. So two axes — tail latency at short token counts, and concurrency at burst scale. There are typical tradeoffs: batching helps throughput but can increase tail. Priya, can you explain how Redwood approaches streaming and tail mitigation?
[01:05] Priya: Sure. Our runtime supports continuous streaming with smallish batching windows optimized for p95. We do automatic KV/prefix caching for repeated prompts — that reduces token generation work and warms the KV cache for attention layers. Quick caveat: the auto-batching window may add a few ms of queuing at very low QPS, but under burst we maintain high utilization so batching helps. Also, we support model variants and quantized builds — quantization lowers perf but may slightly change output quality.
[01:35] Miguel: When you say KV cache, is that the key-value cache for the attention layer? Sometimes I've seen docs call it KV cache and other places K V cash in transcripts — sorry.
[01:43] Priya: Yes KV cache, key-value. The transcription sometimes mangles it yeah.
[01:47] Sara: For us, the critical number is p95 for 10-40 tokens. What do typical numbers look like on your Hosted API for a 7B-ish open model?
[01:58] Priya: Typical p95 for 7B quantized on our Hosted tiers with streaming enabled is in the 120-220ms range for the first token onward depending on sequence length and network hop. Important to note network from mobile -> CDN -> region adds variance. We often recommend a CDN edge + shortest region routing.
[02:19] Miguel: If we went Dedicated with reserved GPUs in our preferred region, how much shaving can we expect?
[02:25] Priya: Dedicated removes noisy neighbor variance and shortens cross-tenant routing. Practically, for your token profile you'd often see 20-40% tail improvement in p95 and more consistent 99th percentiles. Also, Dedicated lets you pin quantization and kernel selection for a more stable profile.
[02:41] Tanya: Are there tradeoffs with autoscaling during surges? We don't want cold-starts causing big spikes.
[02:47] Alex: We're big on burst capacity and warm pools. For Dedicated, you can configure warm reserve and fast burst policies; for Hosted we have burst capacity across multi-tenant pools but it's probabilistic and sometimes subject to regional limits. Priya can add specifics.
[02:59] Priya: Yes, dedicated pools can be set with a warm buffer; autoscaler steps happen in seconds but cold startup for a GPU-backed model could be 30-90s without warm pools. For the 10-20 minute surges you described, warm reserve is the recommended approach.
[03:15] Miguel: Okay. On the benchmark — we want to run token/sec profiling and a streaming p95 test across 500/1k/2k concurrent streams. What's the best way to collect realistic traces?
[03:25] Priya: The standard approach is to give us a request distribution and a small sample payload set. We'll provide a load script (k6/locust style) and an example harness that records per-token timings and server timestamps (we prefer unix epoch ms). That gives us frontend -> edge -> model -> token timings.
[03:39] Alex: We'll send the benchmark template after this call. Miguel, we'll need a sample of your request mix and any warm prefixes.
[03:47] Miguel: We'll pull that together. Also, security — we need to ensure route PII doesn't leave our VPC. How does Redwood handle PII in Hosted?
[03:57] Alex: Hosted uses tenant isolation but it's not VPC-level. For strict PII controls we recommend Dedicated in a customer VPC or Private deployment. We have KMS integrations for key whitelisting and optional HSM support for Private. We will share SOC 2 docs and network diagrams.
[04:12] Sara: Good. Any latency penalty for using customer-managed KMS?
[04:17] Priya: Minimal. KMS calls are for key unwrap at model load/encryption boundaries; they don't hit per-request path. If you do envelope encryption correctly, per-request decryption is handled locally.
[04:25] Tanya: Something we worry about is tokenization variance across model variants — if we quantize or change kernels, does that change tokenization or token counts that affect cost?
[04:36] Priya: Tokenization is model-dependent but independent of quantization. Quantization affects compute, not tokenization. Where you can see differences is if you switch models (e.g., 7B vs 13B) or model families. Our optimize tool can recommend model candidates that preserve quality while saving cost.
[04:50] Miguel: On costs, if we accept a little more tail latency but reduce cost, what's the common trade customers pick?
[04:56] Alex: For many, they accept slightly higher p95 for non-critical messages and keep a lower SLO for critical confirmations. Another pattern: use small models for quick confirmations (cacheable) and a larger model for planning. Redwood supports automated routing policies to pick model by route.
[05:12] Sara: Let's talk numbers. For 600 concurrent, what compute footprint do you need for 7B quantized to keep p95 <250ms? And what about 2k concurrent?
[05:23] Priya: Rough ballpark: for short-token surgical calls, a single GPU can serve ~300-600 concurrent streaming sessions depending on sequence length and batching behavior for 7B quantized. For 2k concurrent you look at 3-5 GPUs with Dedicated pools and careful batching/tuning. We'll produce a capacity matrix specific to your token distribution.
[05:42] Miguel: Do you support multiplexing multiple model instances on a single GPU? We run mixed workloads.
[05:47] Priya: Yes, our runtime can schedule multiple model shards and context lengths on a GPU. Multiplexing helps utilization but makes tail engineering more complex; Dedicated lets you reserve workloads to limit that.
[05:59] Tanya: Regarding streaming metrics — we need per-token timing and p95 of first-byte and last-byte. Does Redwood expose those?
[06:07] Alex: Yes Console exposes token-level latency breakdowns, per-route and per-token step timings. We can generate traces and send a raw CSV if you prefer.
[06:15] Miguel: Great. Also we might run a local on-prem test later, what's the process for Private deployment? Any rough lead time?
[06:22] Priya: Private deployments vary — air-gapped/on-prem could be 8-12 weeks for packaging, network setup, and KMS/HSM integration depending on customer infra. Many customers start with Dedicated in region and then move to Private once requirements firm up.
[06:36] Sara: For the pilot, our timeline is tight — we'd like to validate before our next sprint planning the week of Feb 10. Can Redwood run the 1-week pilot starting Feb 3?
[06:45] Alex: We can do that. We'll need your sample traces and an approved NDA addendum for volume testing. We'll slot SE time to run hosted and dedicated runs in parallel.
[06:55] Miguel: Last technical Q — what about fallback strategies? If Dedicated pool saturates, do you failover to Hosted? Is that automatic?
[07:02] Priya: We support policy-driven fallback. You can set a priority list: Dedicated -> Hosted regional -> Hosted global. Fallback can be automatic with rate limiting or explicit error codes depending on your preference. There are mechanisms to avoid token duplication in streaming when failover occurs but it needs careful client handling.
[07:18] Tanya: That's important — we need idempotency in retries.
[07:21] Priya: We'll include retry best-practices in the playbook.
[07:25] Alex: Ok wrapping up, quick recap of owners and next steps. We'll send the benchmark template and a proposed schedule for Feb 3-10 pilot. Priya will draft the Dedicated vs Hosted capacity matrix. Miguel, you'll provide request distribution and traces by Jan 31. Alex will share SOC2, KMS, and network docs.
[07:42] Sara: Sounds good. Also please include a cost estimate for 100k p95 requests/month as a baseline.
[07:49] Alex: Will do. Anything else?
[07:52] Miguel: No, thanks everyone. Looking forward to the benchmark.
[07:55] Alex: Thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the pilot.
[08:00] Priya: Bye.

Transcript notes: occasional mis-attribution and word swaps present (e.g., K V cash -> KV cache). Some timestamps approximate.
